lesson.title: Changing a Value's Type Without Changing What It Means
lesson.summary: Type conversion turns a value of one type into an equivalent value of another type, either automatically or on request, and not every conversion is safe or even possible.
lesson.body:
Type conversion is the general process of turning a value of one type into an equivalent value of another type. The core types covered so far in this unit, int, float, bool, and str, each represent overlapping information in different forms: the integer 3, the float 3.0, and the string "3" can all describe the same underlying quantity, three, but Python treats them as distinct objects that support different operations. Type conversion is what lets a program move a piece of data from the form it happens to be in to the form a particular operation actually needs.

Conversions come in two flavors, which the next two lessons in this unit cover individually. Implicit type conversion happens automatically, without you writing any special code, whenever Python can convert a value safely and unambiguously; this is what happens when 3 + 1.5 quietly becomes a float calculation. Explicit type casting happens when you call a conversion function yourself, such as int(), float(), or str(), to state directly what type you want a value converted to. Both flavors do the same underlying job, producing a new value of a different type, but they differ in who decides that a conversion should happen: the language, or the programmer.

Not every conversion is safe, and this is where type conversion becomes something you have to reason about rather than assume will just work. Converting an int to a float always succeeds, since every whole number has an exact decimal equivalent, as in float(5) producing 5.0. Converting a float to an int, however, truncates any fractional part rather than rounding it, so int(9.9) produces 9, not 10, which can silently lose information if you are not expecting it. Converting a string to a number only works if the string actually looks like a valid number: int("42") produces 42, but int("forty-two") raises a ValueError, because Python has no reasonable way to interpret those characters as a number.

Here is a short trace showing a conversion chain:

raw = "19"
age = int(raw)
older = age + 1
message = "Next year you will be " + str(older)
print(message)

raw starts as the string "19". Calling int(raw) converts it to the integer 19, stored in age. Adding 1 produces the integer 20, stored in older. Since + between a string and an integer is not allowed, str(older) is used to convert 20 back into the string "20" before it can be joined onto the rest of the message. The final print displays "Next year you will be 20". Every step in that chain is a deliberate type conversion, chosen because a specific operation, arithmetic in the middle, string concatenation at the end, required a specific type in order to work.

Because conversions can fail, real programs often guard them with error handling rather than assuming they will always succeed. Wrapping a conversion in a try and except block, such as trying int(raw) and catching a ValueError if it fails, lets a program respond gracefully to bad input, printing a helpful message instead of crashing outright. This matters most whenever the value being converted originally came from outside the program itself, such as a user typing at a keyboard or data read from a file, since a program has no control over what that source actually sends it, and cannot simply assume every value will already be in the type it expects.
